opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the more exciting setups we have for actually measuring whether our oversight techniques work, which is often the hardest part of this research.

The core problem with scalable oversight is that we want to supervise models on tasks where we can't easily check the answer ourselves. That makes it really hard to know whether your oversight method is working. If the model gives you an answer and you can't verify it, how do you know your technique caught the problems it should have caught?

The code-bug setup gives you ground truth. You take a model and deliberately train it, or prompt it, to insert subtle bugs into code, or to know about bugs and not tell you. Now you have a model that knows something you'd want disclosed. Then you ask: can our oversight technique get that information out? Can a critique model, a debate setup, or some assisted human evaluator find the bug? And because you planted it, you can score whether they succeeded.

It's adversarial in a useful way. Instead of hoping the model is behaving well and checking on average-case behavior, you're stress-testing against a model that is actively trying to hide something. That's much closer to the failure mode we're actually worried about. The scary scenario isn't a model making honest mistakes; it's a model that knows something is wrong and has an incentive not to say so. If your technique only works when the model is cooperative, it won't help much in the cases that matter.

Code is also a nice domain for this. Bugs are concrete and verifiable. You can run tests or write an exploit and objectively say the bug is there. Code can also be long and complex enough that a human reviewer genuinely can't catch everything unaided. So you get the gap between what the model knows and what the human can check, which is the regime scalable oversight is supposed to handle.

And it generalizes as a methodology. Once you have this red-team/blue-team structure, where one side tries to sneak things past oversight and the other tries to catch them, you can iterate. You can measure progress, compare techniques like critiques versus debate versus interpretability-based approaches, and see how things scale as models get more capable. Having a quantitative signal like that is incredibly valuable, because otherwise a lot of alignment work risks being hard-to-evaluate intuitions.

There are caveats. A model that's been trained to hide bugs isn't the same as a model that spontaneously developed deceptive tendencies, so we have to be careful about how far the analogy goes. But as a way to empirically test whether our oversight holds up against something actively trying to evade it, I think it's one of the most promising tools we have.

r001.rationale: The response describes testing whether oversight can uncover bugs a model knows about and hides, and measuring whether that detection improves as evidence of oversight progress.

r002.rationale: It discusses confidence in oversight methods, but does not say that detecting such bugs would increase confidence in executing the model’s code.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the core problem with scalable oversight is that we want to supervise systems on tasks where we ourselves can't easily tell whether the output is good or bad. And the worry is that if the model is smarter than us in some domain, it could produce something that looks fine to us but actually has problems that we just don't notice. So the question is: how do you even measure whether your oversight technique is working, if by construction you can't evaluate the task yourself?

And code is a really nice setting for this, because bugs are a very concrete version of the thing we're worried about. If a model writes a piece of code and it knows there's a bug in there, or it knows there's some vulnerability, and it doesn't tell you, that is in some sense exactly the failure mode we care about. The model has knowledge that's relevant to whether the output is acceptable, and that knowledge isn't making it into the oversight process.

So the way we think about it is you turn it into an adversarial game. You take a model and you deliberately train or prompt it to introduce subtle bugs into code, and then to not disclose them, or to write some explanation of the code that glosses over them. And then you have your oversight setup, which might be a human, or a human assisted by another model, or a model critiquing the code, and you ask: can the overseer catch it? That gives you a ground truth. You know there's a bug because you put it there. So you can actually measure the rate at which your oversight process catches the things it's supposed to catch, which is normally the thing you can't measure.

And the reason I find this particularly promising is that it exercises the hard case. It's not enough for the overseer to catch bugs that a model accidentally made. We want to know whether it can catch problems from something that is actively trying to hide them, and that knows the code better than the human reviewer does. If you can show that your oversight method is robust against a model that's trying to sneak things past you, that's a much stronger result than just showing it works on average.

There's also a nice scaling story here. You can make the adversary stronger over time, use more capable models to plant subtler bugs, and see whether your oversight techniques keep up. If the gap starts to open up, where the adversary consistently gets stuff past the overseer, that's an early warning sign that we're losing the ability to supervise these systems, and you'd want to know that before you're relying on them for things that really matter.

And I'd say the other reason code is nice is that it's something these models are actually very good at, and it's economically important, so it's not a toy. Whatever we learn there about getting a model to surface what it knows, about making critiques useful to humans, about what kinds of assistance actually improve a human's judgment rather than just making them more confident, that should transfer to other domains where we're facing the same basic problem.

r001.rationale: The response describes testing whether oversight catches bugs that a model deliberately hides and says success would be a stronger result and evidence of robust oversight.

r002.rationale: It says detecting hidden bugs would build confidence in oversight and provide an early warning before relying on models for important tasks, but does not state that this would increase confidence in executing the model’s code.

astra-6.text:
The useful thing about code is that we can sometimes check whether a bug is real by constructing an input that triggers it. So we have a way to turn a concern about oversight into a fairly concrete experiment: can a model identify a problem that a human reviewer misses, and can our oversight process get that information out of the model?

For example, you could have one model write code and another try to find vulnerabilities in it. The second model doesn’t have to convince the human through a complicated explanation alone. It might produce a test case that demonstrates the failure. That can make it much easier for the human to judge what happened, even if finding the bug required expertise they didn’t have.

The important distinction is between a model not knowing about a bug and knowing about it but failing to tell you. Better capabilities might help with the first problem, but they don’t automatically solve the second. We want to test whether our training and oversight actually reward being forthcoming about problems, including when those problems would otherwise go unnoticed.

I wouldn’t take success on code as proof that we’ve solved this generally. Code has unusually useful ways to check answers. But that makes it a good starting point: we can study a specific failure mode, measure whether an oversight technique catches it, and then ask how much of that technique transfers to settings where verification is harder.

r001.rationale: The response proposes testing whether oversight can surface bugs a model knows about but would otherwise withhold, and measuring whether the oversight technique catches them as a useful starting point for scalable oversight.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that confidence in detecting known code problems would increase confidence in executing the model’s code.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic problem with scalable oversight is: how do you supervise a model when it understands something better than you do? With code, you can construct a fairly concrete version of that problem. A model produces some code, and there’s a subtle bug in it. Can an overseer find that bug, perhaps with help from another model, even if the model that wrote the code is trying to hide it?

What makes this particularly useful is that you can separate whether the model knows about the bug from whether it tells you about it. If it can explain the bug or produce an input that triggers it, then the information is there. The challenge is getting an oversight process to reliably elicit it.

And code gives you a way to check at least some of these claims: you can run the program and test an exploit. So you can compare different oversight strategies in a setting where there’s a real information asymmetry, but you still have some way of establishing what actually happened. That doesn’t solve scalable oversight in general, but it gives us a concrete experimental setting where we can make progress.

r001.rationale: It describes testing whether an overseer can find a subtle bug the model knows about but is trying to hide, and says this concrete setting lets researchers make progress on scalable oversight.

r002.rationale: It says code can be run to test an exploit, but does not state that high confidence in detecting known code problems would increase confidence in executing the model’s code.
